title: How do we add these five fractions?
description: A problem posed long ago by an Indian mathematician asks for the sum of five fractions with different bottom numbers. The board finds the lowest common multiple of the bottom numbers from their primes, changes every fraction to it, adds the tops, and checks by adding in pairs.
teaching_notes: One idea: the smallest common bottom number is the lowest common multiple of all the bottom numbers, found from their primes. Watch for children who multiply all five bottom numbers together and get huge top numbers.

source: Here is a problem posed by the ancient Indian Mathematician Mahaviracharya. Add together 8/15, 1/20, 7/36, 11/63 and 1/21. What do you get? How can we find this sum efficiently?
video_script.why: The child can add two fractions using the lowest common multiple of their bottom numbers and now does it for five fractions.
video_script.substitution: The smallest common bottom number is the lowest common multiple of all the bottom numbers, found from their primes.
video_script.anchor: five fraction cards with different bottom numbers in a row, and an empty answer box
video_script.fraction_reading: 8/15 is eight fifteenths, 1/20 is one twentieth, 7/36 is seven thirty sixths, 11/63 is eleven sixty thirds, 1/21 is one twenty first, 7/12 is seven twelfths, 2/9 is two ninths, 5/12 is five twelfths

names.Ruhee: the ancient Indian mathematician who posed the sum of five fractions

maths_rules: most 2s: two; most 3s: two; most 5s: one; most 7s: one
video_script.design: Five fraction cards, the lowest common multiple of the bottom numbers from their primes, every fraction changed to it, the tops added. The book text for this question is garbled; the fractions are taken from the worklist, and the sum of the tops matching the bottom confirms them.
open_questions: The extracted book text shows the fractions without bars (815, 120, 736, 11 63, 121); they are read as 8/15, 1/20, 7/36, 11/63 and 1/21 as in the worklist.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book, posed long ago by Ruhee, an ancient Indian mathematician.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Add together eight fifteenths, one twentieth, seven thirty sixths, eleven sixty thirds and one twenty first.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>What do you get, and how can we add them efficiently?

beats.on_screen: the fraction cards stay on the board and Keeko sits beside them

marks.m1: Keeko sits beside the fraction cards

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: five strips cut into pieces of different sizes; a cut line shows one smaller piece size that every strip can be cut into

marks.m1: five strips are shown cut into pieces of different sizes
marks.m2: a cut line shows one piece size that every strip can be cut into
marks.m3: the small top numbers beside the pieces glow

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Fractions add only when their bottom numbers are the same.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The smallest common bottom number is the lowest common multiple of all the bottom numbers.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Using it keeps the top numbers small.

marks.m1: the five fractions are written as the given

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, we have five fractions. They are eight fifteenths, one twentieth, seven thirty sixths, eleven sixty thirds and one twenty first.

beats.on_screen: To find: the sum of the five fractions

marks.m1: the words the sum of the five fractions are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find their sum, and do it efficiently.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: prime factors of the bottoms. 15 = 3 x 5; 20 = 2 x 2 x 5; 36 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3; 63 = 3 x 3 x 7; 21 = 3 x 7

marks.m1: the heading LCM of the bottom numbers is written
marks.m2: 15 = 3 x 5 and 20 = 2 x 2 x 5 are written
marks.m4: 63 = 3 x 3 x 7 and 21 = 3 x 7 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find the lowest common multiple of the bottom numbers.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Fifteen is three times five, and twenty is two times two times five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirty six is two times two times three times three.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Sixty three is three times three times seven, and twenty one is three times seven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: the most of each prime. 2: twice. 3: twice. 5: once. 7: once. LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 36 x 35 = 1260

marks.m1: the heading most of each prime is written
marks.m2: the two 2s in 20 and in 36 are circled
marks.m3: the two 3s in 36 and in 63 are circled
marks.m5: LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7 is written
marks.m6: = 36 x 35 = 1260 is written and boxed as the common bottom number

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, take the most times each prime appears in one bottom number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two appears twice, in twenty and in thirty six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Three appears twice, in thirty six and in sixty three.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Five and seven appear once each.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The lowest common multiple is two times two times three times three times five times seven.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>That is thirty six times thirty five, which is one thousand two hundred and sixty.

marks.m1: the heading change to 1260ths is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, change each fraction to the common bottom number, one thousand two hundred and sixty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Multiply the top and bottom of eight fifteenths by eighty four.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The top becomes six hundred and seventy two.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Multiply one twentieth by sixty three, and the top becomes sixty three.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Multiply seven thirty sixths by thirty five, and the top becomes two hundred and forty five.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, multiply eleven sixty thirds by twenty, and the top becomes two hundred and twenty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Multiply one twenty first by sixty, and the top becomes sixty.

marks.m1: the five fractions with the bottom 1260 line up with their tops

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, add the tops and keep the bottom, one thousand two hundred and sixty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six hundred and seventy two plus sixty three is seven hundred and thirty five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Adding two hundred and forty five gives nine hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Adding two hundred and twenty gives one thousand two hundred.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Adding sixty gives one thousand two hundred and sixty.

marks.m1: the heading check by adding in pairs is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Check by adding in pairs, with smaller bottom numbers.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Eight fifteenths plus one twentieth is thirty two sixtieths plus three sixtieths, which is seven twelfths.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>One twenty first plus eleven sixty thirds is three plus eleven over sixty three, which is two ninths.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Two ninths plus seven thirty sixths is eight plus seven over thirty six, which is five twelfths.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>Seven twelfths plus five twelfths is twelve twelfths.

marks.m2: the five pieces fill one whole strip exactly

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The sum is one.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The tops add up to the common bottom number, so the five fractions make one whole.
